author: Augustine

passages.original: Sunt in Ecclesia lapides pretiosi , et semper fuerunt, docti , abundantes sciemia et eloquio et omni instructione Legis. Pretiosi plane lapides isti sunt : sed ex eorum numero quidam aberraverunt ab ornamento mulieris hujus. Quantum enim pertinet ad doctrinam ct eloquium unde fulgetf, lapis pretiosus erat Cyprianus : sed mansit in hujus ornamento. Lapis pretiosus erat Donatus : sed resiluit a compage ornamcnri. tile qui mansit, in ea se amari voluit 2 : illc qui inde excussus est, præter illaln nomen sibi quæsivit.
passages.english: There are precious stones in the Church, and there always have been: learned men, abounding in knowledge and eloquence and in all instruction in the Law. These are plainly precious stones; but of their number some have strayed from the adornment of this woman. For as far as concerns the learning and eloquence with which he shone, Cyprian was a precious stone; but he remained in her adornment. Donatus was a precious stone; but he sprang away from the setting of the adornment. The one who remained wished to be loved in her; the one who was shaken out of it sought a name for himself apart from her.
passages.notes: Several scanning errors corrected silently (sciemia = scientia, ct = et, fulgetf = fulget, ornamcnri = ornamenti, tile = ille, illaln = illam). The 'woman' is the Church, from the preceding context.

passages.original: Regnum hoc, quod siiie fine dedisti, o qai nihil dedisti, in terra cst, an in caelo ? Utique in terra. Et si esset in coelo, Cœlum et terra transient (Luc. xxi, 33). Transient quæ fecit ipse Deus; quanto citius quod condidit Romulus ? Forte si vellemus hinc exagitare Virgilium, et insultare, quare boc dixerit; in parte tolleret nos, et diceret nubis : Et ego scio ; sed quid facerem qui Romauns verba vendebam , nisi bac adulatione aliquid promitterem quod falsum erat ? Et tamen et in boc cautus fui, quando dixi , «Imperium sine fine dedi,» Jovem ipsorum induxi, qui hoc diceret.
passages.english: This kingdom, which you have given without end, O you who have given nothing, is it on earth or in heaven? On earth, surely. And even if it were in heaven, "Heaven and earth will pass away" (Luke 21:33). The things that God himself made will pass away; how much more quickly what Romulus founded? Perhaps if we wanted to harass Virgil over this and mock him for saying it, he would take us aside and say to us: "I know that too; but what was I to do, I who was selling words to Romans, except promise by this flattery something that was false? And yet even in this I was careful: when I said, 'I have given empire without end,' I brought in their Jupiter to say it."
passages.notes: 'Rome' readings of scanning errors (siiie = sine, qai = qui, boc = hoc, nubis = nobis, Romauns = Romanis) corrected. 'in parte tolleret nos' taken as 'take us aside'.

passages.original: Hanc partem sibi elegcrat etiam illa Maria, quæ ministrante et circa murium ministerium occupata sorore sua, scdebat ad pcdes Domini, et otiosa verbum ejusaudiebat. Joannesstabat, rat:sed illa corde stabat, et ille " humilitate sedebat. Statio enim significat permansionem ; sessio, humilitatem. Et ut sciatis quia statio permansionem significat, hanc permansionem dicitur diabolus non habuisse; de quo dictum est: Ille homicida erat ab initio, et in veritate non stelit (Joan.
passages.english: This part Mary too had chosen for herself, who, while her sister was serving and busy with much serving, sat at the Lord's feet and at leisure listened to his word. [...] stood, [...]; but she stood in heart, and he sat in humility. For standing signifies remaining; sitting, humility. And so that you may know that standing signifies remaining, the devil is said not to have had this remaining; of whom it was said: "He was a murderer from the beginning, and did not stand in the truth" (John 8:44).
passages.notes: 'circa murium ministerium' read as 'circa multum ministerium' (Luke 10:40). The sentence 'Joannesstabat, rat:sed illa corde stabat, et ille humilitate sedebat' is corrupt; 'Joannes stabat' seems garbled and the genders (illa/ille) look confused—probably originally something like 'she sat in humility and stood in heart'. Translated literally where possible; the opening words are left as lost.
